strengths: The media path is genuinely byte-free for the thing that matters, and this is the single property that makes the economics work. Video upload hands the browser a TUS ticket and gets out of the way (app/api/admin/uploads/route.ts:122 returns tusEndpoint); playback returns a URL, not a stream (app/api/playback/token/route.ts:57); posters answer with a 302 to the CDN rather than proxying (app/api/poster/[titleId]/route.ts:66-70). The one exception, photographs, is capped at 4MB with the reasoning written down at app/api/admin/catalogues/[id]/photos/route.ts:19-31 — the storage-zone write password cannot go to the browser, so megabytes proxy and gigabytes do not. docs/SCALE-PLAN.md:195-198 claims compute cost is unrelated to video hosted; the code backs that claim. A rewrite in Go or Java would not improve this, because the application is already not in the data path.

Cache invalidation is complete, which is the part of a read cache that is normally wrong. revalidateCatalogue has 15 call sites covering every write an operator can observe — publish, catalogue edit, title edit, title retry, photo add and delete, transfer, claim, platform term and offline changes, the couple's own edits — plus the Bunny webhook (app/api/webhooks/bunny/route.ts:68) and the reconcile cron (app/api/cron/reconcile/route.ts:87). The two deliberate omissions are argued in place rather than forgotten: draft autosave does not invalidate (app/api/admin/catalogues/[id]/modules/route.ts:9-10) and a published preset is frozen instead (app/api/admin/presets/[id]/route.ts:13-19).

Index coverage matches the query shapes. catalogues.slug is unique (supabase/migrations/0001_initial_schema.sql:38), so the hot guest lookup at lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1338 is a unique-index probe, not a scan. titles (catalogue_id, published, category, sort_order) and photos (album_id, sort_order) serve the bundle reads; 0007_storage_only.sql:20-21 adds covering indexes on size_bytes specifically so the storage check does not fetch rows; 0001:119 is a partial index on processing titles for the reconcile job. Someone worked the access paths out rather than indexing by reflex.

The obvious N+1 was already found and fixed where it hurt first. catalogueCounts (lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1091-1140) draws the studio console's list in four queries regardless of how many weddings the org has, and app/admin/page.tsx:53-55 records why. The studio console — the surface an actual paying customer uses daily — does the right thing.

The performance budgets are enforced by CI, not merely documented. .github/workflows/ci.yml runs check:bundle (the 150KB gzip first-load gate) and check:vitals (LCP and CLS) on every push, and the workflow file itself carries a post-mortem of the time a decorative test-reporter step silently skipped five real gates for days. scripts/check-bundle.ts:82-84 even warns when a budget is met by under 5% headroom.

Failure modes are consistently chosen toward safety rather than convenience. getEntitlements fails to the *low* cap on a lookup error (lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1223-1240 — 'erring toward you have the free tier is recoverable; erring toward unlimited is a bill'). consumeCredit is a compare-and-set claim loop, so two publishes cannot both spend the last credit (:788-815). The data cache carries a generation key (lib/catalogue-cache.ts:38) so a deployed schema change cannot serve a stale row shape. None of these come free with a language choice.

findings.title: The guest page is not ISR-cached, and the capacity plan is built on the assumption that it is
findings.evidence: app/c/[slug]/page.tsx:21 declares `export const revalidate = 3600`, but the page's first call is resolveAccess, which reads cookies at lib/catalogue-access.ts:57. lib/catalogue-cache.ts:13-17 says so in plain words: reading cookies 'opts the route out of static generation entirely ... So the render stays per-request'. docs/SCALE-PLAN.md:81-83 rests its headroom arithmetic on the opposite: 'the guest page is ISR-cached (revalidate = 3600, invalidated on publish), so 300 guests hitting one link mostly hit the edge cache, not a function.' The code wins. There is no route cache on the guest surface; there is a data cache, which is a different thing and only removes the Supabase round trips.
findings.why_it_matters: The bill is not the risk here — Vercel invocations are cheap. The risk is the one moment the product is judged. CLAUDE.md's definition of done is a film starting in under 1.5 seconds on 4G. A wedding link goes out on WhatsApp and 300 phones open it inside a few minutes: every one of those is a full server render on a possibly cold Node instance, not an edge cache hit. That burst is the product demo, and the document Sandeep is using to decide whether the stack holds says it is absorbed by the CDN when it is not.
findings.fix: Two moves, in order. (1) Correct docs/SCALE-PLAN.md §3 today so the decision is made on real numbers — the sentence at line 81 is false and it is load-bearing. (2) Make the route cacheable: the only reason it is dynamic is three cookie reads (locale, profile, passcode grant). Move the passcode and locale decision into middleware.ts, which already runs on every request, and have it set a header the page reads; render the shell statically and hydrate the per-guest bits (profile, resume position) client-side from the existing /api/progress GET at components/streaming/CatalogueProvider.tsx:108. That returns the guest page to a true edge hit.
findings.effort: 0.5 day for the doc correction; 3-5 days for the static shell

findings.title: The 10-second playback heartbeat is roughly 12x the whole function budget the scale plan assumes, and costs five Supabase round trips each
findings.evidence: components/streaming/useProgressHeartbeat.ts:5 sets HEARTBEAT_MS = 10_000 and POSTs to /api/progress every tick while playing. app/api/progress/route.ts:9 is force-dynamic, so every tick is a function invocation, and each does at least five Supabase round trips: getProfile and getTitle (:38-41), getProgress (:50), upsertProgress (:53), recordPlayEvent (:65), plus requireServableCatalogue. docs/SCALE-PLAN.md:16 assumes 300 guests x 20 minutes; 20 minutes at one beat per 10s is 120 beats, x300 guests is 36,000 invocations for a single wedding. docs/SCALE-PLAN.md:70-71 puts the *entire* system at 30,000 function invocations a month for ten weddings. The heartbeat alone is 360,000.
findings.why_it_matters: Two costs, and the second is the dangerous one. The invocation count means the true Vercel ceiling is around 25 weddings a month, not the 333 the document reports — an error of 13x in the number Sandeep would use to decide whether this stack survives. More seriously: 300 concurrent guests at one beat per 10s is 30 requests/sec sustained, each fanning out to five PostgREST calls, so ~150 queries/sec against a Supabase Pro instance that is two ARM cores, concurrently with the un-cached page renders from the previous finding. That is the database saturating on the wedding evening, which shows up to the couple as a page that will not load.
findings.fix: Batch on both sides. In components/streaming/useProgressHeartbeat.ts:5 raise HEARTBEAT_MS to 30_000 and accumulate deltas into an array, sending one request with several samples (the beacon on pagehide at :71 already guarantees nothing is lost on exit). Then collapse the five queries into one Postgres function: `record_play_event` already exists (called at lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1806) — extend it to validate profile-and-title-belong-to-catalogue and upsert playback_progress in the same statement, so a heartbeat is one round trip instead of five. That is a 3x reduction in invocations and a 15x reduction in database calls.

findings.title: The Supabase driver silently ignores liveOnly, so guests see unpublished photographs in production and no test can catch it
findings.evidence: The interface at lib/db/repository.ts:343 is `listPhotosForCatalogue(catalogueId: string, options?: { liveOnly?: boolean })`, documented at :338-342 as 'the guest's view ... photographs a catalogue Publish has carried live'. The memory driver honours it (lib/db/memory-repository.ts:924: `.filter((p) => !options?.liveOnly || p.liveAt !== null)`). The Supabase driver does not: lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1625-1632 declares one parameter and its query has no live_at predicate, even though the column exists (supabase/migrations/0012_content_waits_for_publish.sql:11), the mapper reads it (supabase-repository.ts:107, :340), and publishCatalogueContent writes it (:975-977). lib/catalogue-cache.ts:65 passes `{ liveOnly: true }` and gets every photograph back. TypeScript accepts a narrower implementation signature, so `tsc --strict` is green and all 659 tests pass — against the memory driver.
findings.why_it_matters: Today, on the five live catalogues, a photograph is visible to guests the moment it finishes uploading rather than when the studio publishes. That is the exact failure N-57 was built to prevent, and it is the kind a couple notices before you do. The scalability point is worse than the bug: this is what the two-implementation seam costs. The suite's confidence does not transfer to production, the drift class is unbounded, and it grows with every method added to a 1,869-line driver. That is the mechanism by which a codebase stops being trustworthy, and it is not fixed by changing language.
findings.fix: One line in lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1625 — accept `options` and chain `.not('live_at', 'is', null)` when `options?.liveOnly`. Then close the class: package.json already has a `test:integration` script; write one contract suite that runs the same assertions against MemoryRepository and SupabaseRepository and run it in CI against a throwaway Supabase branch. Every method the two drivers both implement should be covered by the same test, once.
findings.effort: 2 hours for the bug; 2 days for the shared contract suite

findings.title: The nightly usage cron is O(catalogues x titles) serial provider calls in one function with no maxDuration, and it degrades silently
findings.evidence: app/api/cron/usage/route.ts:51 loads every catalogue, :58 loads every title per catalogue, and :65 awaits `provider.getUsage(title.providerId)` one title at a time — fully sequential, no concurrency, no batching. `grep -rn maxDuration app/ lib/ next.config.ts vercel.json` returns nothing, so the route runs on Vercel's default duration. The try/catch at :95 is per-catalogue, so a wall-clock kill mid-loop produces no error at all — just a rollup that covered some catalogues and not others.
findings.why_it_matters: This is within twelve months at the stated 10 weddings/month: 120 catalogues x ~8 titles is ~960 serial HTTPS calls to Bunny. At 150ms each that is about 2.5 minutes, past the default ceiling. When it dies the job_runs row says nothing useful and there is no record of which catalogues were skipped. What stops working is the delivery alert at :80-90 — the only automated signal that a wedding's link has leaked and is burning Bunny delivery. docs/SCALE-PLAN.md:151-156 says building metering is what lets you enforce anything; a metering job that silently covers a random subset is worse than none, because it reads as done.
findings.fix: In app/api/cron/usage/route.ts: add `export const maxDuration = 300`; replace the nested serial awaits at :57-69 with a bounded-concurrency map (8 at a time is safe against Bunny's rate limits); and give rollUp a cursor — take `listAllCatalogues` with a limit and an `updated-since` order so a run that does not finish resumes on the next pass rather than always starting from the same end. Report `skipped` in the returned object so a partial run is visible in job_runs. Do the same for app/api/cron/reconcile/route.ts:50-90, which has the identical serial shape.

findings.title: The platform console does one database round trip per org (N+1) and reads every catalogue with no order and no limit
findings.evidence: app/admin/platform/page.tsx:31 is `Promise.all(orgs.map((org) => repository.creditBalance(org.id, now)))`. creditBalance (lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:817-819) delegates to listCredits (:756-764), which is one PostgREST GET per org. app/admin/platform/studios/page.tsx:27 does the same over the filtered studio list. The same page calls listAllCatalogues (lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1815-1819) — `select('*')` with no `.order()` and no `.limit()` — and app/admin/platform/catalogues/page.tsx:25 does too, then filters and sorts the whole platform's catalogues in JavaScript at :27-37.
findings.why_it_matters: At 6 orgs this is invisible, which is why it is here. At 100 studios it is 100 sequential HTTPS calls to build one page; at 1,000 the dashboard times out. This is the surface Sandeep himself uses to run the business, so it fails for him before it fails for anyone else — and it fails at exactly the point where the business is finally working. The missing `.order()` on listAllCatalogues is the sharper edge: Supabase's PostgREST caps responses at 1,000 rows by default, and an unordered query means the 1,001st wedding is not merely missing, it is missing non-deterministically.
findings.fix: Add `creditBalancesFor(orgIds: string[]): Promise<Record<string, CreditBalance>>` to lib/db/repository.ts and implement it in both drivers as one `credits` select with `.in('org_id', orgIds)` folded in memory — the same shape catalogueCounts already uses successfully at supabase-repository.ts:1091. Then give listAllCatalogues an explicit `.order('included_until')` and a `{ limit, cursor }` parameter, and move the search at platform/catalogues/page.tsx:27 into an `.ilike()` filter so the database does the filtering.

findings.title: Nothing is paginated, and PostgREST's default row cap will truncate list reads without an error
findings.evidence: lib/db/supabase-repository.ts is 1,869 lines and contains five `.limit()` calls in total — :705, :728, :799, :1067, :1556 — every one of them either a single-row pick or an explicitly-bounded list. listCatalogues (:1075), listOrgs (:379), listAllCatalogues (:1815), listPhotosForCatalogue (:1625), listTitles (:1390), listCredits (:756) and listDomains (:630) are all unbounded `select('*')`. There is no cursor, offset or range anywhere in the repository interface (lib/db/repository.ts).
findings.why_it_matters: Supabase sets PostgREST's max-rows to 1,000 by default. Past that, a list read does not error — it returns 1,000 rows and a 206 that supabase-js does not surface. The result is a catalogue list that quietly stops growing, a usage cron that quietly stops covering new weddings, and a platform dashboard whose counts are quietly wrong. Every one of those failures is invisible until someone reconciles by hand against the Bunny bill. It bites at 1,000 catalogues, which is roughly the 1,000-weddings-a-month case, and it is much cheaper to add the parameter now than to retrofit pagination into 60 API routes and 40 pages later.
findings.fix: Add an optional `{ limit?: number; cursor?: string }` to the list methods on lib/db/repository.ts that can grow without bound — listAllCatalogues, listOrgs, listCatalogues, listPlatformAudit — defaulting to 200 with an explicit `.order()` on a stable key, and thread `next_cursor` through the three platform pages. Add an integration test that seeds 1,100 catalogues and asserts the second page is reachable; without that test the cap is invisible in every environment you can afford to run.

findings.title: `.in()` with an unbounded id array will return HTTP 414 on a large studio, breaking its own console home page
findings.evidence: catalogueCounts builds id arrays with no chunking and passes them straight into PostgREST filters: lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1106 `.in('catalogue_id', ids)`, :1122 the same, and :1132 `.in('album_id', [...albumCatalogue.keys()])`. The same unbounded pattern appears at :976, :1013 and :1272. PostgREST encodes filters into the query string, so the request line grows with the array; a UUID costs roughly 40 bytes encoded and Supabase's gateway rejects request lines past about 8KB.
findings.why_it_matters: That is roughly 200 ids per query. A studio with 70 weddings at three albums each crosses it on the album query at :1132, and the failure lands on app/admin/page.tsx — the studio's own console home, the screen they open every day. It manifests as a 414 that neither the error handler nor the ApiError shape anticipates, so the operator sees a blank list rather than a message. The bitter part is that catalogueCounts is otherwise the best-engineered read in the file: it solved the N+1 correctly and then reintroduced the ceiling in the fix.
findings.fix: Either chunk — a six-line `chunk(ids, 100)` helper in lib/db/supabase-repository.ts wrapping the three `.in()` calls and merging the results — or, better, replace the whole method with one Postgres function `catalogue_counts(p_org_id uuid)` that aggregates in SQL and returns one row per catalogue. The RPC path is preferable because it also fixes the row volume: today the method drags every title row and every photo row in the org across the wire to arrive at five integers.
findings.effort: 4 hours to chunk; 1 day for the RPC

findings.title: Every film card on the guest page costs its own dynamic function and two uncached database reads
findings.evidence: app/api/poster/[titleId]/route.ts:8-9 is `runtime = 'nodejs'` and `dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`. Each request does getTitle (:53), getCatalogueById (:58) — both of which go straight to the repository, bypassing lib/catalogue-cache.ts entirely — then resolveAccess (:60), which reads cookies again, then mints a Bunny signature. modules/curated-row/Guest.tsx:29 and modules/continue-watching/Guest.tsx:46 both build `/api/poster/${title.id}?file=preview.webp`, so a title appearing in two rows is two requests. CACHE_S at :28 is 900 seconds against an ASSET_TTL_S of 3600 at :25.
findings.why_it_matters: A guest landing on a catalogue with eight films fires eight to sixteen of these before the page is readable, each a cold-startable Node function doing two Supabase calls for rows that lib/catalogue-cache.ts already has in memory for that same request. It is the second-largest contributor to the invocation count after the heartbeat, and unlike the heartbeat it lands in the critical path of first paint — which is the 1.5-second promise in CLAUDE.md's definition of done.
findings.fix: In app/api/poster/[titleId]/route.ts, replace the getTitle/getCatalogueById pair at :53-58 with a read through getCachedBundle — the title is already in the cached bundle keyed by catalogue, and resolveAccess at :60 already gives you the catalogue. That removes both database calls. Then raise CACHE_S at :28 from 900 to 3000 (still inside the 3600s token TTL) so the browser and Vercel's CDN absorb repeats for the length of a viewing session rather than a quarter of it.

findings.title: Per-instance memory is used for two things that assume they are global: the passcode lockout and the health probe memo
findings.evidence: lib/http/rate-limit.ts:16 is a module-level `Map`, honestly labelled at :4-11 as 'exact on a single instance, approximate across several'. lib/health/probes.ts:28 is a second module-level Map with REMEMBER_MS = 60_000 (:26), and app/admin/platform/page.tsx:33 asserts 'Remembered for a minute by the probes themselves, so the dashboard costs no extra calls.' Both assumptions hold on one instance. The sweep at rate-limit.ts:19-24 also only triggers past 5,000 entries and then walks the entire map inline on a hot path.
findings.why_it_matters: The rate limiter's own doc justifies the trade on the grounds that the passcode gate 'sees single-digit requests per second'. That was true when it only guarded the passcode; app/api/progress/route.ts:33 now calls `enforce` on the heartbeat, which is the highest-volume endpoint in the product. High volume is exactly what makes Vercel warm several instances, so the wedding evening that needs the 5-attempt lockout from doc 05 §4 is the evening it becomes a 5-per-instance lockout — a brute-force window that widens precisely with traffic. Separately, each cold instance re-runs all health probes at a 3-second budget each, so the platform admin's dashboard is slow exactly when they are opening it because something is wrong.
findings.fix: Split the two uses. Keep the in-memory limiter for the heartbeat, where approximate is genuinely fine, and move the passcode bucket to Postgres: a `passcode_attempts (catalogue_id, ip, count, reset_at)` table with an upsert is one round trip on a path that already does several, and it is correct across instances. Change the call site in app/api/passcode/route.ts only — lib/http/rate-limit.ts:10-11 already anticipates this ('swap the store, not the call sites'). For probes, persist each HealthRow to the existing job_runs-style table rather than a Map.

findings.title: Four of the six cron routes are not scheduled by the platform, and the one that matters most for cost hangs off GitHub Actions
findings.evidence: vercel.json:8-17 registers exactly two crons: /api/cron/reconcile and /api/cron/usage. The other four routes exist — app/api/cron/lifecycle, notify, warnings, synthetic — and app/api/cron/notify/route.ts:19-23 explains why ('Vercel's Hobby plan allows two cron jobs ... Adding a third fails the deploy outright'). .github/workflows/notify-drain.yml:59, :77 and :101 drives lifecycle, warnings and notify from GitHub instead. notify's own comment at :29-32 records that concurrent drains double-send, because drain reads, sends, then marks, and the 0009 CHECK constraint has no 'sending' state to claim a row with.
findings.why_it_matters: The lifecycle job is the only thing that moves a catalogue down the lapse ladder to `cold`, and docs/SCALE-PLAN.md:101-121 identifies storage that is never reclaimed as the only cost curve that compounds — the difference between roughly 72,000 and 2.18 lakh rupees a year by year five. That job's schedule currently depends on a GitHub Actions cron, which GitHub documents as best-effort, delays under load, and disables automatically on a repository with 60 days of inactivity. The single most expensive long-run process on the platform is driven by the least reliable scheduler in the stack.
findings.fix: docs/SCALE-PLAN.md:32 already budgets for Vercel Pro, which lifts the cron cap. Move all six into vercel.json:8 and delete .github/workflows/notify-drain.yml. Separately, add a 'sending' status to the notifications CHECK constraint in a new migration so drain can claim a row before it sends — that closes the double-send window the comment describes and makes the job safe to run at whatever frequency you like.
findings.effort: 2 hours for the crons; 4 hours for the claim status

findings.title: Play events accumulate forever at one row per heartbeat, and the retention column that exists is read by nothing
findings.evidence: supabase/migrations/0001_initial_schema.sql:179 creates play_events, indexed at :188 on (catalogue_id, at desc). app/api/progress/route.ts:65 inserts one per heartbeat where deltaS > 0 — one row per guest per ten seconds of watching. supabase/migrations/0006_entitlements.sql:25 declares `retention_months integer`; grepping retention_months across lib/ and app/ returns only the migration. Nothing prunes.
findings.why_it_matters: docs/SCALE-PLAN.md:175-182 calls this 'a year three problem rather than a year one problem' on the basis of 0.16 GB across 60 weddings. That estimate does not appear to account for a ten-second heartbeat: 300 guests x 20 minutes is about 36,000 rows for a single wedding, so 60 weddings is a couple of million rows plus index — meaningfully more than the document assumes, though still not urgent against Supabase Pro's 8 GB. The real cost is not the disk; it is that the table grows unboundedly under the index that the analytics read uses, so the studio's own stats page gets slower every month with no event that explains why.
findings.fix: Add a delete to runLifecycle in lib/lifecycle.ts — `delete from play_events where at < now() - interval '13 months'` — and read the per-entitlement override from the retention_months column that 0006 already provides rather than hard-coding. Thirteen months keeps a full year-on-year comparison. While there, correct docs/SCALE-PLAN.md:177 with the measured row count rather than the estimate.

findings.title: Both language dictionaries ship in the guest bundle, against a budget with 4KB of headroom
findings.evidence: lib/i18n.ts:9 exports a single `dictionary` object holding the complete `en` and `hi` maps across 424 lines. components/streaming/CatalogueShell.tsx:1 is `'use client'` and imports createTranslator from it, as does components/streaming/ModuleRenderer.tsx:1, so both locales land in the browse chunk that every guest downloads. lib/budgets.ts:17 sets BROWSE_FIRST_LOAD_KB = 150 and scripts/check-bundle.ts:7 records the last measurement at 146KB — 'four kilobytes of headroom, with nothing watching'.
findings.why_it_matters: Every English guest downloads the Hindi strings and every Hindi guest downloads the English ones, and the cost grows monotonically with every string the product adds. It is perhaps 3KB gzipped today — not a crisis, but against 4KB of headroom it is most of the remaining budget, and it is the one line item that no feature work can avoid growing. The guest's locale is already resolved on the server at lib/guest-locale.ts before the client tree renders, so the work of shipping both is pure waste.
findings.fix: Split lib/i18n.ts into lib/i18n/en.ts and lib/i18n/hi.ts with the shared createTranslator/resolveLocalised logic in lib/i18n/index.ts. The server already knows the locale, so pass the resolved message map into CatalogueShell as a prop instead of importing the dictionary from the client component. That removes the unused locale from the bundle and turns a growing cost into a flat one.
